blocks.p: Dear Stephen, people used to write letters. You put words on paper and sent them to someone you loved, and then you waited, sometimes for weeks, not knowing. The waiting was half the letter. Nobody waits for anything now. Some days I think that’s the worst thing they did to us.
The courier had been waiting in the Thorne office for eleven days, and in all that time, Lyda said, he had not once taken off his coat.

He was standing when Sol came up the stair, as if he had been standing the whole eleven days: a young man, slight and smooth-faced, in the plain grey of a lay clerk of the episcopal house, with both hands pressed over one breast of the coat. Teo had found him on the pier asking for the bishop and had very nearly put him back on the ship. Now Teo sat on the corner of Lyda’s desk with his arms folded, watching him the way a dog watches a stranger in the yard.

“He wouldn’t give it to me,” Lyda said. She did not get up. “He wouldn’t give it to Tobin. He said by hand. I asked him whose hand. He said the bishop’s. I told him we didn’t have one. He waited anyway.”

The clerk was staring at Sol. Sol knew the look; he had seen it go through the crowd in the Bounty Market like a draft through a room. The young man’s eyes went to the grey, which was all through Sol’s hair now, and to the lines at the corners of his eyes and mouth, and stayed there, and something in his smooth face flinched and could not stop flinching.

“Your Grace,” he said. His voice cracked on it. “I’m Matthis Rennet. I serve in the episcopal house. I was asked to put this into your hand and no one else’s, and to wait for an answer, and not to read it.” He swallowed. “I haven’t read it.”

He took his hands from his coat and drew out a folded packet and held it out. It was paper, real paper, heavy and cream-colored and soft at the folds, and it was sealed in white wax with a bishop’s seal Sol knew as well as his own. Across the front, in ink, in a hand that had plainly cost its writer a great deal of trouble, it said: Tarren. By hand. From the east hall.

Sol took it. He broke the seal and unfolded the sheets and held them up to the lamp, and the writing swam. He moved it farther off, and then farther, until his arms were nearly straight, and the letters steadied a little and were still too small.

Lyda watched him do it. She said nothing at all. She got up and went down the stair, and came back a few minutes later with a pair of old wire-framed lenses from Lucan’s surgery, and put them into his hand, and sat down again.
He put them on. The letter came clear.
Tarren,

Forgive the hand. I had to learn. There is no paper in Sion; my clerk found this in the archive of the first council, and I practiced on the backs of their minutes for a month, so if anyone ever wonders what the first council decided about the eastern provinces, I’m afraid I’ve written over it. It is the strangest thing, making a word with your arm. It doesn’t go anywhere. It just stays where you put it.
I signed at the evening office. I want you to know that my hand was perfectly steady. It has not been steady since.

They asked me about you for three days. They were very kind. They asked whether you had said anything to me, any word, and I said no, and that was true, wasn’t it? You didn’t say it. You only said the old man’s name.

I went under in the autumn. The east hall, the good chairs. Yours was empty. No one had thought to take your name off it, and I found I couldn’t ask them to. Afterward there was no one on the steps to tell me what they’d taken. I woke up missing something, Tarren, just as I told you I would. I thought that when I woke I would at least know what. I don’t.

Your deacon was renewed in the spring. He serves at Concord now and is very happy. I asked him whether he missed you. He said, “Oh, the bishop will be back,” and then he looked at me as if I’d asked him something in another language.
The failures go on. No one says relays anymore.

I have questions I can’t ask anyone. I find I can’t ask them on paper either. Paper keeps things. A bishop may open a sealed line from the episcopal house to any panel in the colonies, unlogged, for a quarter of an hour, for confessions of a delicate kind. I have never used it. I’m told the Thorne office on Philippa has a panel. On the last night of the quarter, at the twenty-second hour by your clock, I will open the line. If you aren’t there I’ll understand. I think I’ll be relieved. I know I’ll be sorry.
Don’t write anything back that you wouldn’t want read. Everything I read goes up the line. I have only lately understood what that means.
Sol read it twice. Then he took the lenses off and folded them and sat for a while holding the letter on his knee, with the lamp hissing and Teo pretending not to watch him.
“May I?” Lyda said.
He gave it to her. She read it quickly, the way she read freight manifests, and then again, slowly, and handed it back.
“He signed your death order,” she said.
“Yes.”
“And now he’d like a quarter of an hour on my panel.”
“It’s your panel.”
“It is.” She looked at him across the desk with her sharp, tired, unimpressed face. “They know where you are anyway. You’ve told me so. To the meter.”
“Yes.”
“So why the paper?”
“Because he’s frightened,” Sol said.

The courier was waiting for an answer, and there was paper still folded inside the packet, two blank sheets that Aurelian had sent for the purpose. Sol borrowed a pen from Lyda’s desk and sat down at the end of it.

He could not remember when he had last written by hand. He had signed everything with a thought. He put the pen to the paper and his hand knew what to do before he did, and what came out was not the small slanting script of Stephen’s copy or the careful loops of Aurelian’s, but square, upright capitals, each letter separate, like the labels on a diagram. He looked at them for a moment. He did not know where they had come from.
Aurelian. I’ll be there. I am old now; you may not know my voice.
He began to sign it Tarren, and stopped, and wrote Sol.
Matthis Rennet took it in both hands as if it were hot, and put it inside his coat, and left on the morning ship for Plenty. He did not take off his coat on the way down the stair, either.
The quarter ended four days later.

The panel stood in a corner of the long office, an old voice-only commercial set with a scratched brass grille, which the Thorne line used for arguing with Plenty about freight rates. Lyda had sent Teo home. She had not gone herself. She sat at the far end of the room with a ledger open under the lamp and a pen in her hand, and when Sol looked at her she said, “It’s my panel,” and went on writing.
At the twenty-second hour exactly, the panel chimed.
For a moment there was nothing on the line, only a faint hush, the sound of a very great distance. Then a voice said, out of long habit, “Remember the Mountain.”
Sol did not answer. He could not have.
“No,” Aurelian said, after a moment. “I suppose not.” A breath. “Hello, Tarren.”
“Hello, Aurelian.”
“You sound...”
“Old.”
“I was going to say tired.” There was something in the pause that was nearly his laugh. “Are you? Old?”
“Forty-nine, my doctor says. He measures me with calipers. I’ve gone grey. I need lenses to read, which you’d know if you’d seen me with your letter. Your hand is terrible, by the way.”
The laugh came then, the real one, quick and warm and startled out of him, the laugh from every long dinner in the Holy City since their ordination, and Sol closed his eyes to hear it.
“I practiced for a month,” Aurelian said.
“It shows.”
Then the line was quiet again. When Aurelian spoke, his voice had dropped. “What does it feel like?”
Sol thought of the old man by the spice stall in Abundance, white-haired and bent, and of how badly he had wanted to go and ask him exactly that.

“My knees hurt in the mornings,” he said. “I’m cold more often. In the afternoons I get tired, and I sleep, and I dream. Everything is heavier. I think that’s the whole of it. Every day costs something now, so every day is worth something.”
“That sounds dreadful.”
“It is, a little. I wouldn’t give it back.”

A long silence. Then, lower: “There’s a thing I have to tell you before I lose the nerve for it. They send me the returns now. I asked for them. The chaplains on your worlds send them up: who went into the water, and whose hands. Most of them are only names. One wasn’t.” A breath. “A man on Korinna went to the port chaplain of his own accord. He’d been in the water in the harbor, he said, and then he’d fallen away, and the hum had come back on, and once it was on he could feel that he’d done a wrong thing and ought to put it right. So he confessed it. He said the hum had taught him that was the honest thing to do.” Another breath. “A dice-runner. Morrow.”
Sol’s hand had closed on the brass grille. “Dace.”

“They flagged him. The chaplain couldn’t hold him, not out there, but he could put him on a church hull going in, for assessment, and the man went willingly. He thought he was being forgiven. They had him at the Mercy house on Plenty inside the month.” Aurelian’s voice had gone very careful, the way it went when he was reading from something. “The return said Released. Nothing under it; there never is. I know what we say, that Mercy has its own door. So I asked to see him. They gave me a resting light, Tarren. I sat in front of it an hour. There was no one in it.”

Sol said nothing. He was on a bollard in the Korinna harbor among the hulls, in the heat and the smell of frying, learning that it was possible to grieve for a man who was still alive. He had thought that was the whole of the lesson.
“I signed nothing,” Aurelian said. “I want you to know that. I only read the name. I’ve read it every night since.”
“He shook my hand,” Sol said. “On the way out. He wished me well.”
The line hushed between them, the whole distance of it.
“Tell me about him,” Aurelian said at last. “The one whose name you wouldn’t say to me.” Then, quickly: “No. Don’t say it. If you say it, I’ll have heard it. Tell me about him without it.”

So Sol told him, as plainly as he could, in the corner of the dark office with his hand on the brass grille. A man who sat down by a well because he was tired. Who touched a leper when no one else would come near. Who found a boy thrashing on the ground in front of a crowd that had already decided he was dead, and took him by the hand and lifted him up. Who stood at his friend’s grave and wept, though he knew what he was about to do. Who was killed by careful, reasonable men in good robes, for the good of the people, and asked his father to forgive them while they were still driving in the nails.
“Hale said that,” Sol said. “At the end. He said it about me.”
Aurelian said nothing.
“And afterward a woman went to his grave and found it empty, and stood outside it crying, and he came and asked her why. Not to stop. Why. And then he said her name.”
The silence went on so long that Sol thought the line had failed. Then Aurelian spoke, very low.

“I was at the Hierarch’s table last week. Someone mentioned you. Everyone was very kind about it; they said it was a sickness, that it wasn’t your fault. I went back to my rooms afterward and sat down on the floor.” He gave a short breath. “I don’t know why. I sat on the floor for an hour, Tarren. I think I was trying to do what you did. I couldn’t find it. Where do you find it?”
“I didn’t,” Sol said. “It found me.”

“Does he forgive a man who knew?” It came out fast, as if it had been waiting behind his teeth the whole time. “You didn’t know. Hale said so. They don’t know what they’re doing (Luke 23:34). What about a man who knew exactly what he was doing, and signed anyway, and his hand was steady?”
Sol was quiet for a moment.

“There was a man who had walked with him for three years,” he said. “On the night they took him, this man followed and stood by a fire in the courtyard, while inside they were beating him. And three times someone asked the man whether he was one of his friends, and three times he said, I do not know the man.”
He heard Aurelian’s breath stop.
“I never knew a Stephen Hale,” Aurelian said.
“Yes.”
“What happened to him?”

“He went out and wept bitterly. And afterward, when it was all over, the one he’d denied came and found him on a beach at dawn, cooking fish over a fire, and asked him three times whether he loved him.” Sol’s own voice was not quite steady now. “Once for every time.”
There was a sound on the line he did not at first recognize. Then he did. It was the sound a man makes when he puts his hand over his own mouth.
“What would I lose?” Aurelian said at last, muffled.
“Everything. The east hall. Renewal. Your face. You’d grow old. You’d die.”
“I’ve had this face for four hundred years.”
“I know. I was fond of it too.”
“And what would I have?”
“Him,” Sol said. “And your own head. And grief. You’d be allowed to grieve. It’s worse than I thought it would be, and better.”

“Tarren.” The voice had gone thin and quick. “Do you understand what I’m doing? I’m in a sealed room, on a sealed line, and none of it makes the least difference, because I’m the leak. Everything you say to me goes into my head, and my head is copied every hour of every day. They don’t read the backups without a reason. I’m giving them one. I’m giving it to them now, while you talk.” His breath was coming fast. “They asked me about you for three days.”

“Then say the name,” Sol said. “Say it and mean it. Turn, and let someone take you down into the water. The name breaks the noise, and the rest comes after, and then it goes quiet, and they can’t read you anymore. I promise you, it goes quiet.”
At the far end of the room, Lyda’s pen had stopped.

The silence on the line stretched. Sol could hear him breathing, fast and shallow, across all that distance, and behind it, very faint, a bell somewhere in the Holy City. Then there was the edge of a sound, the beginning of a hard consonant, caught in the throat.
It stopped there.
“I can’t.” Aurelian’s voice broke on it. “I can’t, I can’t. I’m not you. I was never brave, Tarren. I only ever stood next to you.”
“I wasn’t brave. Someone came for me anyway.”
“I know,” Aurelian whispered. “I signed the order for it.”
The panel gave a soft tone. A minute left on the quarter hour.
“I couldn’t take your name off the chair,” Aurelian said, all in a rush. “Did I say? In the letter? I couldn’t.”
“You said.”
“Where will you be? Tell me where. So I can think of you somewhere. I can’t think of you nowhere; I’ve tried.”
“Wherever the Thorne ships go,” Sol said. “Daphne in the spring, I think, and then Galatia. Write to me here. They’ll find me.”
At the far end of the room, Lyda lifted her head.
“Tarren,” Aurelian said, fast and low, “if they ask me...”
The line closed.

Sol sat with his hand on the brass grille. It was warm from the lamp. The hush of the distance was gone, and the room was only a room, with the yard lights showing through the shutters and the lamp hissing on Lyda’s desk.
“Jory has to hear it tonight,” he said. “No one who’s been in the water crosses inward. Not past Plenty. Not for a chaplain, or a kind voice, or anything.”
“He’ll have it within the hour.” Lyda had not moved. “And your friend will tell them.”
“He might.”
“And you’ve told him where you’ll be in the spring.”
“They’ve always known where I am.”
“Knowing where a man is and knowing where he’s going are different things.” She closed the ledger. “I run ships. I know the difference.”
“He’s frightened.”
“Frightened men are the ones who do things.”
“I was frightened,” Sol said. “Someone came anyway.”
Lyda looked at him for a long moment across the dim room, and he could not read her face. Then she got up and took her coat from the hook.
“Go to bed, Bishop,” she said. “You look a hundred.”
“Forty-nine.”

“Go to bed.” On her way past she reached down and took Lucan’s lenses from where he had pushed them up into his hair, folded them, and put them into his breast pocket, as if she had been doing it for years. Then she went down the stair, and he heard the yard door close behind her.
He did not go to bed. He knelt on the boards in front of the dead panel, as he had once knelt before a Pearl, with nothing in his hands.

The noise came almost at once. It came in his own voice, catching on the same word over and over like a door on a bad hinge. His hand was steady. Steady. His hand was steady. Steady hands sign. Steady.

He did not say the name. He found that he did not want to spend it on this. He let the voice go on, and stayed on his knees under it, and prayed first for Dace Morrow, who had shaken his hand and wished him well and gone willingly up a ramp, and who was nowhere now that anyone could point to. On the bollard in the harbor he had grieved for a man who was alive. He had not known a man could be grieved for twice. Then he began, for the first time in his life, to pray for Aurelian.

It had never once occurred to him that Aurelian needed it, smooth and fond and amused at the edge of his life, the one who made the jokes at the Hierarch’s table. He had never seen the fear. It had been there the whole time, he understood now, under every light word, the way the hum had been under every silence.

“He’s afraid,” Sol said into the dark office, over the top of that other voice, which was his own. “He was always the one who was afraid, and I never once saw it. Find him. Ask him three times if you have to. Don’t hold it against him.”

Steady, the voice said, more faintly. Steady. It went on a while longer, thinning, like someone talking on in a room everyone else has left. Sol did not answer it. When he got up off his knees, a long time later, it had stopped, and he could not have said when.
Far away, in a white room in the Holy City, his oldest friend was sitting with his hand over his mouth, and every word Sol had said to him that night was going up the line.
